question: Which original studies compare competing against a believed-human opponent with a known-computer opponent in competitive games, with enjoyment-related outcomes?

S2.title: Does It Matter with Whom You Play?

S3.title: Psychophysiology of Digital Gaming: Non Co-Located Opponent

S5.title: How do we think machines think? An fMRI study of alleged competition with an artificial intelligence

S6.title: When people are defeated by artificial intelligence in a competition task requiring logical thinking, how do they make causal attribution?

S7.title: Increasing motivation in robot-aided arm rehabilitation with competitive and cooperative gameplay

S8.title: A multisession evaluation of an adaptive competitive arm rehabilitation game

S9.title: Playing online games against computer- vs. human-controlled opponents: Effects on presence, flow, and enjoyment

S10.title: Metabolic changes playing active video game (Wii Boxing) against a human and computer opponent

S12.title: Video Game Violence and the Female Game Player

S13.title: Imaging the intentional stance in a competitive game

S14.title: Brain Activity Dissociates Mentalization from Motivation During an Interpersonal Competitive Game

S15.title: The Anterior Insula Tracks Behavioral Entropy during an Interpersonal Competitive Game

S16.title: Differential reward responses during competition against in- and out-of-network others

S17.title: Can machines think? Interaction and perspective taking with robots investigated via fMRI

S18.title: Responses of medial and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex to interpersonal conflict for resources

claims.text: [1] population: players of a tank shooter in fMRI
[1] exposure: alleged human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer opponent
[1] results: ventral striatum tracked self-rated pleasure; vmPFC and dorsal striatum responded more to winning against a human; design fMRI
[2] population: players of a video game; exposure: computer, friend or stranger as opponent; comparator: computer; design: self-report, interbeat intervals, facial EMG
[2] results: more presence, engagement and positive emotion against humans; abstract does not state whether participants were deceived
[3] population: players of a video game with non co-located opponents; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
[3] results: more positive emotion, arousal, presence and engagement against a human; design: EMG, interbeat intervals, skin conductance
[4] population: twenty Call of Duty players; exposure: same agent told to be agent or avatar; comparator: opponent told to be an agent
[4] results: arousal differences when the enemy was first met, mixed measures later, some players not convinced of humanity
[5] population: participants in rock-paper-scissors fMRI; exposure: believed human, humanoid robot or random computer; comparator: random computer
[5] results: activity human > robot > random; mPFC and right TPJ responded to the human only; design fMRI
[6] population: participants in three experiments (N = 74, 788 and 500); exposure: competing against an AI or a believed human in a logical-thinking task; comparator: believed human
[6] results: re-challenge did not differ in two experiments and was lower in the AI condition in one
[9] population: players of online games; exposure: computer- vs human-controlled opponent; comparator: computer-controlled
[9] results and design: not available, only the title (presence, flow and enjoyment) was read
[13] population: volunteers in stone-paper-scissors PET; exposure: believed to play the experimenter or a computer; comparator: computer
[13] results: only anterior paracingulate cortex more active under the intentional stance; design PET; no enjoyment measure
[14] population: participants in a competitive gain-loss game; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
[14] results: network sensitive to opponent type (human > computer); design: two fMRI studies
[15] population: participants in matching pennies; exposure: told human or computer with the same algorithm; comparator: computer
[15] results: opponent affected behavioural entropy; anterior insula tracked entropy; design fMRI
[16] population: participants in a card-guessing game; exposure: close friend, confederate or random number generator; comparator: random number generator
[16] results: striatal responses stronger for social than non-social competitors in an exploratory analysis; design fMRI
[17] population: participants in an iterated prisoner's dilemma; exposure: computer, functional robot, anthropomorphic robot or human partner; comparator: computer partner
[17] results: more fun and competition with human-likeness; medial frontal and right TPJ activity rose; design fMRI
[19] population: participants in matching pennies; exposure: human, android, robots or computer; comparator: computer
[19] results: impressions of agents modulated dorsal and ventral pathway activity; design fMRI
[7] population: 30 unimpaired and 8 stroke participants; exposure: competitive (human) air-hockey mode; comparator: single-player against the computer
[7] results: unimpaired participants preferred two-player modes; those liking competition put in more effort; Intrinsic Motivation Inventory
[8] population: rehabilitation participants over several sessions; exposure: three sessions against a human then one against a computer; comparator: computer
[8] results: friend or relative at home showed higher enjoyment and exercise intensity; clinic pairs no significant difference
[20] population: participants in an online image-recognition game; exposure: told computer- or human-controlled opponent (always computer); comparator: presumed human
[20] results: copresence higher against a computer-controlled opponent in one condition; outcome is social presence
[10] population: Wii Boxing players; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
[10] results: no difference in heart rate or oxygen consumption
[12] population: female game players; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
[12] results: human opponent increased aggressive thoughts; presence the other outcome
[18] population: participants in resource conflicts; exposure: human vs computer partner; comparator: computer
[18] results: more sharing with a human partner; design fMRI
Executive Summary: fMRI tank-shooter study with alleged human and computer opponents found ventral striatum activity tracked self-rated pleasure
Executive Summary: two psychophysiology studies compared computer, friend and stranger opponents and found more positive emotion, presence and engagement against humans
Executive Summary: the non co-located study also found more positive emotion, presence and engagement against humans
Executive Summary: Call of Duty experiment told players the same agent was an agent or an avatar and measured arousal
Executive Summary: rock-paper-scissors against believed human, humanoid robot or random computer gave engagement-like brain activity human > robot > random
Executive Summary: re-challenge after defeat by an AI or believed human gave a mixed result across three experiments
Executive Summary: rehabilitation-game studies compare human competition with playing alone against the computer using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory
Executive Summary: second rehabilitation-game study uses the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory over multiple sessions
Finding 2 verdict: established for mentalizing differences; open for reward
Finding 3 verdict: open; behavioural engagement results are mixed
Finding 4 verdict: probable that agent human-likeness is a continuous moderator; no experiment isolates it for enjoyment

conclusion: A small, mostly pre-2018 literature shows human opponents raise presence, arousal and mentalizing activity, with sparse direct enjoyment and reward evidence; the 60-call cap was reached, so the list is probably incomplete.
